problem: Robots navigating unknown indoor spaces shared with humans from a monocular RGB camera have to anticipate human motion. Classical pipelines (detect, track, predict, plan) need reliable human state estimation, which is hard with narrow-FOV monocular sensors. End-to-end learned policies are sample-inefficient and overfit to their training system. Earlier sim-trained methods either had no humans in training (e.g. LB-WayPtNav) or used textureless humans unsuitable for RGB learning.
motivation: Real service robots must plan around people whose goals and dynamics are unknown, and collecting real human interaction data raises cost, privacy and logistics problems. The paper observes that photorealistic rendering of synthetic humans keeps motion cues in the image (leg spread, toe direction). Combined with an optimal-control expert that has privileged information, this lets a perception network learn human-aware waypoints entirely in simulation and transfer zero-shot to reality.
key_idea: Train a CNN to predict human-aware waypoints from a single RGB image, supervised by an MPC expert with full map and human-trajectory knowledge on photorealistic HumANav renderings of synthetic humans in real building scans; a model-based spline planner and LQR controller then track each waypoint.
insight: Keeping model-based planning and control in the loop and learning only waypoints gives much higher success and far smoother motion than regressing velocities end-to-end (80.52% vs 52.60% success; jerk .60 vs 3.71 m/s³). Training on dynamic humans rather than static scenes adds ~13% success over LB-WayPtNav. Two data-generation choices matter: penalizing human proximity only when the human is visible in the current frame (80.52% vs 68.18% for the always-penalize LB-WayPtNav-DH-FOV variant), and photorealistic human textures (gray-textured humans give a ~6% drop). This suggests the reactive network learns image motion cues such as leg spread rather than explicit trajectory prediction. Evidence: on scenarios where the geometry-only Mapping-SH fails, LB-WayPtNav-DH still succeeds 58.33% of the time.
method: Perception CNN: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 (top removed) plus a downsampling conv and 5 FC layers of 128 units with 20% dropout. Image features are concatenated with the egocentric goal position and current linear/angular speed. Input is a 224×224 RGB image; output is a waypoint (x̂, ŷ, θ̂).

Planning & control: a spline-based dynamically feasible trajectory from the current state to the predicted waypoint under 3-DoF unicycle dynamics, tracked by an LQR on the linearized dynamics. It runs for a control horizon H = 0.5 s, then replans from a new image (memoryless).

MPC-based expert: the human is a goal-driven unicycle agent following piecewise-constant velocity, planned by receding-horizon MPC. Its cost combines FMM goal distance, a cubic hinge obstacle penalty on signed distance, and control effort. Given the human's optimal trajectory, the robot's MPC optimizes waypoints with a cost on goal distance, obstacle hinge and human-proximity hinge (high λ3, giving cautious behavior). The full map is known at training time only.

Data sampling heuristics: the human's start is placed roughly along the robot's human-free optimal path to force interaction. Human proximity is penalized only when the human is visible in the robot's current image, so the labels are learnable by a reactive policy.

HumANav data-generation tool: a rendering engine fusing 6000 SURREAL human meshes (controllable gender, texture, body shape, pose, speed) with 7 SD3DIS office building meshes. It renders RGB, depth and surface normals from arbitrary viewpoints, preserving motion-dependent pose cues. Being active/on-policy, it supports rendering along any robot trajectory.

Training: supervised MSE regression on 125K (image, goal, speed) → optimal-waypoint pairs, using Adam (lr 1e-4, weight decay 1e-6, batch 64, 35K iterations) with brightness, contrast, blur and perspective augmentation.

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (ImageNet-pretrained, fine-tuned) CNN waypoint predictor + model-based spline planner / LQR controller
setting.training_data: 125K self-supervised samples rendered with HumANav: 3 SD3DIS training buildings and 4800 SURREAL human identities. Labels come from an MPC expert with full map and human-trajectory knowledge. No real data or human demonstrations.
setting.observation: monocular forward-facing RGB (224×224) + egocentric goal position + robot's current linear/angular speed (robot state from odometry)
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (x, y, θ) tracked by spline trajectory + LQR controller (continuous speed/turn rate), replanning every 0.5 s
setting.simulator: HumANav (SD3DIS building scans + SURREAL synthetic humans)
setting.privileged: none (robot state assumed known via odometry; goal given in global frame)

numbers.eval_set_note: 150 test episodes in a 4th held-out SD3DIS building with held-out human identities; Time/Acc/Jerk computed only on episodes where all methods succeed
numbers.extra: success = within 0.5 m of goal without collision; memoryless single-image policy

numbers_note: HumANav is the paper's own benchmark, not a canonical one. Table II reports LB-WayPtNav-DH Time/Acc/Jerk as 12.94/.09/.64, computed on the smaller subset where both it and the FOV variant succeed; this differs from Table I. The gray-texture ablation is reported only as 'a drop of 6% in the success rate', with no exact number. Hardware results are counts out of 20 trials; no per-experiment table is given. The zero_shot flag on the hardware row means zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, not training-free.
results: In simulation on 150 held-out-building episodes, LB-WayPtNav-DH reaches 80.52% success. That beats LB-WayPtNav without humans (67.53), end-to-end velocity regression (52.60), DWA (63.63) and depth-based Mapping-SH (76.63), with the lowest jerk (.60). It trails only Mapping-WC (94.81), which uses ground-truth depth and ground-truth human state; noise in that state costs Mapping-WC ~7%. On Mapping-SH failure cases LB-WayPtNav-DH succeeds 58.33% of the time and reaches the goal ~6% faster than Mapping-WC. On a Turtlebot 2 with real humans it transfers zero-shot and succeeds in 20/20 trials, versus 7/20 for Mapping-SH and 3/20 for LB-WayPtNav.
limitations: Reactive and memoryless with a narrow forward FOV (~50° on hardware). It cannot reason about humans outside the view or about long-term motion, and it shows trajectory oscillations and sub-optimal paths.

Trained with a single human following piecewise-constant velocity. It fails when it must jointly predict multiple distinct humans' trajectories (e.g. crossing two humans moving in opposite directions).

Assumes accurate robot state estimation and that humans do not react to the robot. The high human-proximity weight yields cautious, not always efficient, behavior; the method is still outperformed by the privileged Mapping-WC in simulation.
